claim: Large uniform surfaces with high spatial predictability strongly suppressed firing yet induced prominent gamma synchronization in macaque V1, particularly when they were colored.
source: We show that large uniform surfaces, which have high spatial predictability, strongly suppressed firing yet induced prominent gamma synchronization in macaque V1, particularly when they were colored.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-2.

claim: Chromatic mismatches between center and surround, breaking predictability, strongly reduced gamma synchronization while increasing firing rates.
source: Yet, chromatic mismatches between center and surround, breaking predictability, strongly reduced gamma synchronization while increasing firing rates.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Differences between responses to different colors, including strong gamma-responses to red, arose from stimulus adaptation to a full-screen background.
source: Differences between responses to different colors, including strong gamma-responses to red, arose from stimulus adaptation to a full-screen background, suggesting prominent differences in adaptation between M- and L-cone signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4-7.

claim: Synchrony signaled whether RF inputs were predicted from spatial context, while firing rates increased when stimuli were unpredicted from context.
source: Thus, synchrony signaled whether RF inputs were predicted from spatial context, while firing rates increased when stimuli were unpredicted from context.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Visual processing relies on an integration of information over space, and an understanding of spatial relationships.
source: Visual processing relies on an integration of information over space, and an understanding of spatial relationships.
evidence: This is a general statement about visual processing supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Integration of visual information takes place in part in a feedforward manner through convergence of neurons with small receptive fields onto neurons with larger RFs in higher areas.
source: This integration takes place in part in a feedforward manner through convergence of neurons with small receptive fields (RFs) onto neurons with larger RFs in higher areas (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Serre et al., 2005; Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000; DiCarlo et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In early visual cortex, neuronal responses to sensory inputs into the RFs are strongly modulated by the spatio-temporal context in which they are embedded.
source: However, already in early visual cortex, neuronal responses to sensory inputs into the RFs are strongly modulated by the spatio-temporal context in which they are embedded.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The firing rates of V1 neurons to stimuli in their classical RF can be increased or decreased by stimuli presented in their surround.
source: For instance, the firing rates of V1 neurons to stimuli in their classical RF (CRF), that is the region in space where stimuli have a strong driving effect, can be increased or decreased by stimuli presented in their surround (Vinje and Gallant, 2000; Rao and Ballard, 1999; Angelucci et al., 2017; Gilbert, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Surround modulation is mediated by recurrent lateral and feedback connections.
source: In terms of anatomy, surround modulation represents a departure from feedforward processing. It is mediated by recurrent lateral and feedback connections, through which a given V1 neuron can be informed about a larger region of space than covered by its CRF (Lund et al., 1993; Gilbert, 1992; Angelucci et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Surround modulation may represent a form of normalization, such that neuronal firing rates are essentially scaled by the amount of drive in the surround.
source: One view on surround modulation is that it merely represents a form of normalization, such that neuronal firing rates are essentially scaled by the amount of drive in the surround (Carandini and Heeger, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Surround modulation may play an important role in contour integration, perceptual filling-in, figure-ground separation, computation of a saliency map, as well as efficient and predictive coding operations.
source: Additionally, it has been suggested that surround modulation may play an important role in various related functions like contour integration (Liang et al., 2017), perceptual filling-in (Zweig et al., 2015; Land, 1959; Wachtler et al., 2003), figure-ground separation (Lamme, 1995), computation of a saliency map (Coen-Cagli et al., 2012; Li, 2002), as well as efficient and predictive coding operations (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Vinje and Gallant, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Theories of efficient coding postulate that surround suppression of neuronal firing contributes to remove image redundancies across space from neuronal representations.
source: Theories of efficient coding postulate that surround suppression of neuronal firing contributes to remove image redundancies across space from neuronal representations (Schwartz and Simoncelli, 2001; Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001; Coen-Cagli et al., 2012; Coen-Cagli et al., 2015; Rao and Ballard, 1999; Barlow, 2001; Vinje and Gallant, 2000; Zhu and Rozell, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Predictive coding theories hold that neuronal responses result from a comparison between predictions from the surround and the inputs into the CRF.
source: Predictive coding theories hold that neuronal responses result from a comparison between predictions from the surround and the inputs into the CRF (Friston, 2005; Rao and Ballard, 1999; Spratling, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: If the modulation of neuronal firing rates arises from specific relationships between stimuli across space, then it might also have important consequences for temporal correlations among neuronal responses.
source: However, if the modulation of neuronal firing rates arises from specific relationships between stimuli across space, then it might also have important consequences for temporal correlations among neuronal responses (Singer and Gray, 1995).
evidence: This is a logical inference supported by a citation.

claim: Recent work has extended the frameworks of efficient and predictive coding beyond firing rate modulations to include neuronal synchronization.
source: Recent work has extended the frameworks of efficient and predictive coding beyond firing rate modulations to include neuronal synchronization (Bastos et al., 2012; Jadi and Sejnowski, 2014; Chalk et al., 2016; Vinck and Bosman, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neuronal synchronization plays a functional role for the encoding and transmission of information, as well as for synaptic plasticity.
source: Neuronal synchronization plays a functional role for the encoding and transmission of information, as well as for synaptic plasticity, and may therefore play an important role in contextual integration processes (Buzsáki et al., 2012; Vinck et al., 2010a; Havenith et al., 2011; Salinas and Sejnowski, 2000; Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001; Sejnowski and Paulsen, 2006; Fries, 2005; Fries et al., 2007; Fries, 2009; Börgers and Kopell, 2008; Kopell et al., 2000; Varela et al., 2001; Wang, 2010; Buzsáki, 2006; Cardin et al., 2009; Singer, 1999; Singer and Gray, 1995; Bressler et al., 1993; O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Bernander et al., 1994; Abeles, 1982; Kempter et al., 1998; Azouz and Gray, 2000; Sohal et al., 2009; Ballard and Jehee, 2011; Ballard and Zhang, 2018; Akam and Kullmann, 2010; Akam and Kullmann, 2014; Palmigiano et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The amplitude of V1 gamma oscillations increases with stimulus size and therefore surround stimulation.
source: A link between contextual modulation processes and V1 gamma-band synchronization is suggested by the finding that the amplitude of V1 gamma oscillations increases with stimulus size and therefore surround stimulation (Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Ray and Maunsell, 2011; Jia et al., 2013b; Chalk et al., 2010; Perry et al., 2013; Jia et al., 2011; Gray et al., 1990, for a detailed discussion, see Vinck and Bosman, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Bastos et al. (2012) and Arnal and Giraud (2012) hypothesized that gamma-band synchronization subserves the encoding and transmission of prediction error signals in the feedforward direction.
source: Bastos et al. (2012) and Arnal and Giraud (2012) hypothesized that gamma-band synchronization subserves the encoding and transmission of prediction error signals in the feedforward direction, and that lower frequency bands carry feedback predictions from higher areas (Bastos et al., 2012; Bastos et al., 2014; Arnal and Giraud, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: According to the prediction error hypothesis, a mismatch between center and surround stimuli should lead to an increase in both firing rates and gamma-band synchronization.
source: According to this hypothesis, a mismatch between center and surround stimuli should lead to an increase in both firing rates and gamma-band synchronization, conveying prediction error signals.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the prediction error hypothesis.

claim: Vinck and Bosman (2016) hypothesized that the amplitude of gamma oscillations in a given column reflects the extent to which classical RF inputs are predictable from the surround.
source: In contrast, Vinck and Bosman (2016) recently hypothesized that (1) the amplitude of gamma oscillations in a given column reflects the extent to which classical RF inputs are predictable from the surround and (2) that gamma-band synchronization among columns with non-overlapping RFs reflects predictability among their visual inputs.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: According to the predictability hypothesis, redundancy between center and surround stimuli should lead to a decrease in firing rates yet an increase in gamma-band synchronization.
source: According to this hypothesis, redundancy between center and surround stimuli should lead to a decrease in firing rates (reflecting efficient coding) yet an increase in gamma-band synchronization.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the predictability hypothesis.

claim: Color is an important feature for object recognition and visual search, and plays a role in social interactions and foraging.
source: The latter is an important feature for object recognition and visual search, and plays a role in social interactions and foraging (Santos et al., 2001; Waitt et al., 2006; Gerald et al., 2007; Bichot et al., 2005; D'Zmura, 1991; Corso et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Colored stimuli have rarely been studied with respect to gamma synchronization.
source: Despite the importance of the color domain in vision, colored stimuli have rarely been studiedwith respect to gamma synchronization (Rols et al., 2001; Shirhatti and Ray, 2018; Brunet et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Uniform surfaces are of particular interest because they contain highly redundant information across a relatively large image region.
source: Furthermore, uniform surfaces are of particular interest because they contain highly redundant information across a relatively large image region.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the properties of uniform surfaces.

claim: The predictability hypothesis suggests that large, uniform surfaces should reliably induce gamma-band synchronization but be accompanied by low neuronal discharge rates.
source: The predictability hypothesis (Vinck and Bosman, 2016) suggests that large, uniform surfaces should reliably induce gamma-band synchronization but be accompanied by low neuronal discharge rates.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the predictability hypothesis.

claim: A chromatic mismatch between center and surround should strongly reduce gamma-band synchronization but increase firing rates.
source: It further suggests that a modulation of center-surround predictability due to a chromatic mismatch (e.g. red center and green surround stimulus) should strongly reduce gamma-band synchronization but increase firing rates.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the predictability hypothesis.

claim: There are likely substantial differences in the way chromatic and achromatic surfaces are processed by area V1.
source: Although uniform chromatic and achromatic surfaces both have a high degree of predictability at the (physical) image level, there are likely substantial differences in the way these surfaces are processed by area V1.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on known differences in visual processing.

claim: V1 surface representations may arise from neurons with RFs at the uniform region of a surface stimulus being directly activated.
source: There are two different ways through which V1 surface representations may arise (Zweig et al., 2015). First, neurons with RFs at the uniform region of a surface stimulus (e.g. the center) may be directly activated.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Surface information may be encoded by neurons with RFs at the edge of the surface, and then propagate toward neurons with RFs at the uniform region of the surface.
source: Second, surface information may be encoded by neurons with RFs at the edge of the surface, and then propagate toward neurons with RFs at the uniform region of the surface (Zweig et al., 2015; Land, 1959; Wachtler et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The relative contributions of local versus edge-derived mechanisms remain largely unknown and likely differ between chromatic and achromatic surfaces.
source: The relative contributions of these two mechanisms (local vs. edge-derived) remain largely unknown and likely differ between chromatic and achromatic surfaces (Zweig et al., 2015; Zurawel et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Activity patterns for achromatic surfaces were consistent with an edge-derived 'fill-in' process.
source: Zweig et al. (2015) have addressed this question by making voltage-sensitive dye recordings of V1 populations and comparing the responses at the surface's center to the edge (Zweig et al., 2015). Activity patterns for achromatic surfaces were consistent with an edge-derived 'fill-in' process (Zweig et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Edge-derived fill-in was not observed for chromatic surfaces.
source: However, this was not observed for chromatic surfaces (Zweig et al., 2015), which could be due to the availability of another, surface rather than edge-based, information source provided by single-opponent cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Contextual interactions likely have a different nature for achromatic than chromatic stimuli.
source: Because contextual interactions likely have a different nature for achromatic than chromatic stimuli, we asked whether there are differences in the contextual modulation of firing activity and gamma-band synchronization between these two classes of stimuli.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on known differences in visual processing.

claim: Multi-unit (MU) activity and local field potentials (LFP) were recorded from the primary visual cortex (area V1) in two macaque monkeys.
source: We recorded multi-unit (MU) activity and local field potentials (LFP) from the primary visual cortex (area V1) in two macaque monkeys, while they performed a fixation task.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Recordings were made using a 64-channel chronic microelectrode array in monkey H and a 32-channel semichronic microelectrode array in monkey A.
source: These recordings were made using a 64-channel chronic microelectrode array in monkey H and a 32-channel semichronic microelectrode array in monkey A (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Classical receptive fields (RFs) of the MU activity were estimated using moving bar stimuli.
source: Classical receptive fields (RFs, referring to classical RFs unless otherwise mentioned) of the MU activity were estimated using moving bar stimuli (see Materials and methods; monkey H: median RF eccentricity 6.2 deg, range 5.2–7.1 deg, median RF diameter 0.48 deg, range 0.26–1.88 deg; monkey A: median eccentricity 5.4 deg, range 3.2–8.5 deg, median RF diameter 0.91 deg, range 0.46–2.3 deg).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods and results.

claim: Compared to a surface stimulus of 6 deg diameter, receptive fields had a median proportional diameter of 0.08 (0.04–0.31, monkey H) or 0.15 (0.08–0.38, monkey A).
source: Compared to a surface stimulus of 6 deg diameter, receptive fields had a median proportional diameter of 0.08 (0.04–0.31, monkey H) or 0.15 (0.08–0.38, monkey A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental results.

claim: The presentation of large, chromatic surface stimuli induced prominent, narrow-band gamma oscillations in LFP power spectra.
source: The presentation of large, chromatic surface stimuli (equiluminant red, green and blue; see Materials and methods) induced prominent, narrow-band gamma oscillations in LFP power spectra (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Gamma-band oscillations were significantly weaker for achromatic surface stimuli compared to chromatic surface stimuli.
source: In comparison, gamma-band oscillations were significantly weaker for achromatic surface stimuli (black or white, maximal contrast to background; Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Gamma peak power changes were stronger for chromatic than achromatic surface stimuli at 97.8% (45 out of 46) of LFP recording sites.
source: Gamma peak power changes were stronger for chromatic than achromatic surface stimuli at 97.8% (45 out of 46) of LFP recording sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The difference in gamma-band oscillations between chromatic and achromatic stimuli is not explained by either luminance or cone-contrast to the FSB.
source: We find that the difference in gamma-band oscillations between chromatic and achromatic stimuli is not explained by either luminance or cone-contrast to the FSB.
evidence: This is a finding from control experiments described in the text.

claim: Removing 100 ms data epochs after each microsaccade did not qualitatively change the LFP results on gamma oscillations.
source: We also removed 100 ms data epochs after each microsaccade and found that the LFP results on gamma oscillations were qualitatively unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from control analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Spike-field phase-locking spectra for chromatic surface stimuli showed a prominent peak in the gamma-frequency band.
source: Spike-field phase-locking spectra for chromatic surface stimuli showed a prominent peak in the gamma-frequency band consistent with the gamma peak in the LFP power spectrum (Figure 1D), whereas phase-locking was significantly weaker for achromatic surface stimuli (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Gamma-synchronization for chromatic stimuli is observed at the level of V1 output spikes, not merely at the level of synaptic currents.
source: The main point of this analysis is that gamma-synchronization for chromatic stimuli is not merely observed at the level of synaptic currents within V1, but also at the level of V1 output spikes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spike-field coherence results.

claim: The presentation of chromatic and achromatic surface stimuli induced short-latency onset transients of similar magnitude.
source: The presentation of chromatic and achromatic surface stimuli induced short-latency onset transients of similar magnitude (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A stronger decrease in MU firing activity over time during continuous stimulus presentation was observed for chromatic than achromatic surface stimuli, starting around 200 ms after the stimulus onset.
source: However, we observed a stronger decrease in MU firing activity over time during continuous stimulus presentation for chromatic than achromatic surface stimuli, starting around 200 ms after the stimulus onset (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: For chromatic surface stimuli, MU firing activity fell below baseline levels.
source: Strikingly, for chromatic surface stimuli, MU firing activity fell below baseline levels (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The reduction in MU firing rates (0.3–1.3 s period) for chromatic as compared to achromatic surface stimuli was observed for 92% of recording sites.
source: The reduction in MU firing rates (0.3–1.3 s period) for chromatic as compared to achromatic surface stimuli was observed for 92% of recording sites.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The late decrease in MU firing was not due to microsaccades.
source: Control analyses in which data epochs after microsaccades were removed indicate that the late decrease in MU firing was not due to microsaccades (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from control analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Large, uniform, chromatic surface stimuli induce low firing activity yet highly gamma-synchronous V1 responses.
source: These findings demonstrate that large, uniform, chromatic surface stimuli induce low firing activity yet highly gamma-synchronous V1 responses, whereas achromatic surface stimuli induce much weaker gamma-band synchronization but relatively more vigorous firing activity (for further interpretation of this finding, see Discussion).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Figure 1.

claim: For chromatic stimuli, increases in stimulus size resulted in increases in induced gamma peak power as soon as the stimulus also covered the surround (i.e. from 2 deg onwards).
source: For chromatic stimuli, increases in stimulus size resulted in increases in induced gamma peak power as soon as the stimulus also covered the surround (i.e. from 2 deg onwards, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: For achromatic stimuli, a gamma peak in the 30–80 Hz band emerged from 2 deg stimulus size onwards and showed no further increase with stimulus size.
source: By contrast, for achromatic stimuli, a gamma peak in the 30–80 Hz band emerged from 2 deg stimulus size onwards and showed no further increase with stimulus size.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: For both achromatic and chromatic stimuli, MU firing activity was highest for 0.5–1 deg stimulus sizes.
source: We observed that for both achromatic and chromatic stimuli, MU firing activity was highest for 0.5–1 deg stimulus sizes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The presentation of a 2 or 6 deg stimulus, increasingly covering the surround, induced strong suppression of MU firing activity as compared to the 0.5 deg stimulus.
source: In contrast, the presentation of a 2 or 6 deg stimulus, increasingly covering the surround, induced strong suppression of MU firing activity as compared to the 0.5 deg stimulus (Figure 2C, rightmost panel).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Surround suppression was stronger for chromatic than achromatic stimuli.
source: This surround suppression was stronger for chromatic than achromatic stimuli (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The addition of the surround stimulus alone induced a rapid suppression of MU firing activity, which was significantly more pronounced for chromatic than achromatic stimuli.
source: We found that this addition of the surround stimulus alone induced a rapid suppression of MU firing activity, which was significantly more pronounced for chromatic than achromatic stimuli (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The relatively strong decrease in firing over time observed for large, chromatic surfaces is at least partially explained by surround suppression.
source: These findings suggest that the relatively strong decrease in firing over time observed for large, chromatic surfaces (Figure 1) is at least partially explained by surround suppression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Figure 2.

claim: For the small RF stimuli, there are no substantial differences on average between chromatic and achromatic surfaces in terms of MU and LFP responses.
source: They furthermore indicate that for the small RF stimuli, there are no substantial differences on average between chromatic and achromatic surfaces in terms of MU and LFP responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Figure 2.

claim: There is a prominent difference in the way chromatic and achromatic stimuli are affected by surround stimulation.
source: Yet, we find a prominent difference in the way chromatic and achromatic stimuli are affected by surround stimulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Figure 2.

claim: Compared to the uniform surfaces, stimuli with a chromatic (blob or annulus) mismatch had higher MU firing activity.
source: We found that compared to the uniform surfaces, stimuli with a chromatic (blob or annulus) mismatch had higher MU firing activity (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A marked decrease in the amplitude of LFP gamma oscillations was observed for the chromatic mismatch compared to the uniform surface stimuli.
source: At the same time, we observed a marked decrease in the amplitude of LFP gamma oscillations for the chromatic mismatch compared to the uniform surface stimuli (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: The result that chromatic mismatch reduces gamma while increasing firing rates was consistent across animals.
source: This result was consistent across animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: For sites with RFs on the outer uniform regions of the stimulus, the MU firing responses did not differ significantly between conditions during the initial transient period.
source: For these sites the MU firing responses did not differ significantly between conditions during the initial transient period (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: During the later sustained response phase, MU firing activity was reduced for the chromatic mismatch stimuli compared to the uniform surface stimulus for sites with RFs on the outer uniform regions.
source: During the later sustained response phase, however, MU firing activity was reduced for the chromatic mismatch stimuli compared to the uniform surface stimulus (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Whenever the RF center covered a large uniform surface region, sustained firing levels were below baseline.
source: Note that whenever the RF center covered a large uniform surface region, either in the uniform stimulus condition or when it covered the surround region of the mismatch stimuli, sustained firing levels were below baseline.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: A mismatch between stimuli at the RF center and the surround can dramatically change the surround influence on responses to the center.
source: These results suggest that a mismatch between stimuli at the RF center and the surround can dramatically change the surround influence on responses to the center.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Figure 3.

claim: The amplitude of gamma oscillations was significantly higher at the center ('RF-on-center') than at the edge of the surface stimulus ('RF-on-edge').
source: We found that the amplitude of gamma oscillations was significantly higher at the center ('RF-on-center') than at the edge of the surface stimulus ('RF-on-edge'), whereas the opposite was observed for MU firing activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Clear gamma-responses were observed for disk stimuli that had their edge blurred with a Gaussian.
source: In one session (monkey H), we also showed disk stimuli that had their edge blurred with a Gaussian (2.5 deg size, 1 deg standard deviation). There were clear gamma-responses also in this case (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: For colored surfaces the amplitude of gamma-band oscillations is commensurate with the 'chromatic' predictability among visual inputs in space.
source: Together, these results indicate that for colored surfaces the amplitude of gamma-band oscillations is commensurate with the 'chromatic' predictability among visual inputs in space, and that gamma-band oscillations are not a mere consequence of input drive to a larger cortical region.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Figure 3.

claim: Gamma strength can be dissociated from stimulus salience.
source: Furthermore, these results suggest that gamma strength can be dissociated from stimulus salience, because the chromatic mismatch condition provided a highly salient stimulus in the RF, but resulted in weaker gamma.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Figure 3.

claim: Gamma-band responses to achromatic and chromatic surface stimuli may have been affected by the use of a gray FSB.
source: Gamma-band responses to achromatic and chromatic surface stimuli may have been affected by the use of this gray FSB, given that the FSB itself may induce adaptation at many levels of the nervous system.
evidence: This is a logical inference about potential confounds.

claim: When the FSB had the same hue as the surface stimulus, there was a nearly complete abolishment of gamma oscillations for blue, green and yellow stimuli.
source: Surprisingly, we found that when the FSB had the same hue as the surface stimulus, there was a nearly complete abolishment of gamma oscillations for blue, green and yellow stimuli (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Red stimuli could still induce detectable gamma oscillations when presented on a red FSB, although the gamma amplitude was strongly reduced compared to the gray FSB condition.
source: Interestingly, red stimuli could still induce detectable gamma oscillations when presented on a red FSB, although the gamma amplitude was strongly reduced compared to the gray FSB condition (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The decrease in gamma-band oscillations with the same hue FSB condition was not due to the large size of the background color stimulation, but was due to the continuous presence of the same-hue background.
source: This indicates that the decrease in gamma-band oscillations with the same hue FSB condition was not due to the large size of the background color stimulation, but that it was due to the continuous presence of the same-hue background.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: For all surface hues, gamma oscillations were amplified when stimuli and FSBs were of opponent color hues.
source: We found that for all surface hues, gamma oscillations were amplified when stimuli and FSBs were of opponent color hues (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Gamma oscillations are dependent on opponency signals along the red-green and the blue-yellow axes.
source: This suggests that gamma oscillations are dependent on opponency signals along the red-green and the blue-yellow axes (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Figure 6C.

claim: The difference among red, green and blue hues observed with a gray FSB could not be replicated when stimuli were presented on a black FSB.
source: Quite surprisingly, the difference among red, green and blue hues that we had observed with a gray FSB could not be replicated when we presented the stimuli on a black FSB (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Compared to the gray FSB condition, gamma-band amplitudes were significantly lower for red and blue surface stimuli and significantly higher for yellow and green surface stimuli when using a black FSB.
source: Compared to the gray FSB condition, gamma-band amplitudes were significantly lower for red and blue surface stimuli and significantly higher for yellow and green surface stimuli (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: For the black FSB condition, gamma-band power was higher for green and yellow than red and blue surface stimuli.
source: Specifically, gamma-band power was higher for green and yellow than red and blue surface stimuli (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: When an FSB of the same hue as the stimulus was compared to a black FSB, gamma was almost abolished for blue, green and yellow, but not for red stimuli.
source: First, when an FSB of the same hue as the stimulus was compared to a black FSB, gamma was almost abolished for blue, green and yellow, but not for red stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: When an FSB of the opponent hue was compared to a black FSB, gamma was enhanced for all colors, but particularly strongly for red.
source: Second, when an FSB of the opponent hue was compared to a black FSB, gamma was enhanced for all colors, but particularly strongly for red (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: For all non-red chromatic FSBs, gamma oscillations were strongly amplified for red surface stimuli.
source: The full matrix of gamma responses for different FSB conditions in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 shows that for all non-red chromatic FSBs, gamma oscillations were strongly amplified for red surface stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Achromatic responses on colored backgrounds were substantially weaker than the reverse (colored stimuli on achromatic backgrounds).
source: Achromatic responses on colored backgrounds were substantially weaker than the reverse (see Section 'Controls for luminance-contrast and cone-contrast').
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Gamma-band responses to surface stimuli depend strongly on the FSB, in a way that follows the color-opponency axes.
source: These data demonstrate that gamma oscillations depend strongly on the FSB, in a way that follows the color-opponency axes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Figure 6.

claim: A commonly used 'default' display of gray introduces adaptation effects that are color-specific.
source: Furthermore, a commonly used 'default' of the display, namely gray, introduces adaptation effects that are color-specific.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Figure 6.

claim: Uniform surfaces tend to adapt the M-cone pathway more strongly than the L-cone pathway, or adaptation of the M-cone pathway has a stronger effect on gamma-band oscillations than adaptation of the L-cone pathway.
source: This suggests that uniform surfaces tend to adapt the M-cone pathway more strongly than the L-cone pathway, or that adaptation of the M-cone pathway has a stronger effect on gamma-band oscillations than adaptation of the L-cone pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from the quantitative model.

claim: The blue-yellow gamma ratio can be predicted by S-cone and L-cone adaptation.
source: We performed a similar analysis for the yellow-blue (L + M S) opponency axis, aiming to predict the gamma ratio of blue over yellow (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from the quantitative model shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Gamma oscillations are mediated not only by opponency signals along the red-green axis, but also along the blue-yellow axes.
source: These findings indicate that gamma oscillations are mediated not only by opponency signals along the red-green axis, but also along the blue-yellow axes, consistent with the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from the quantitative model.

claim: Chromatic surfaces exhibited much stronger gamma-band synchronization yet more suppressed firing than achromatic surfaces.
source: In the present study, we observed that chromatic surfaces exhibited much stronger gamma-band synchronization yet more suppressed firing than achromatic surfaces.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: V1 representations of surface color depend on the direct activation of neurons with RFs in the uniform region of the surface.
source: This finding is consistent with the idea that V1 representations of surface color depend on the direct activation of neurons with RFs in the uniform region of the surface.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Gamma-band synchronization arises from the predictability of visual inputs across space.
source: It further supports the hypothesis that gamma-band synchronization arises from the predictability of visual inputs across space (Vinck and Bosman, 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by a citation.

claim: Color, like stimulus orientation, can be thought of as a 'feature', with predictive value for stimulus features in color space.
source: Together, these data suggest that one could think of color, like stimulus orientation, as a 'feature', with predictive value for stimulus features in color space.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: If the features at the center stimulus are correctly predicted by the surround (context), this results in strong gamma-band synchronization.
source: If the features at the center stimulus are correctly predicted by the surround (context), this results in strong gamma-band synchronization.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Predictability of stimulus luminance by itself in the absence of color information may not be processed as a stimulus feature.
source: On the other hand, predictability of stimulus luminance by itself in the absence of color information, as in the case of a large uniform white stimulus, may not be processed as a stimulus feature.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Luminance by itself, in the absence of color information, may not be sufficient for inducing strong gamma-band synchronization.
source: Luminance by itself, in the absence of color information, may not be sufficient for inducing strong gamma-band synchronization.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Prominent gamma-band synchronization can be generated in response to achromatic stimuli when they have structural features (orientation, frequency, phase) that are highly predictable over space.
source: In contrast, prominent gamma-band synchronization can be generated in response to achromatic stimuli when they have structural features (orientation, frequency, phase) that are highly predictable over space, for example bars and gratings (Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Gray et al., 1989; Chalk et al., 2010; Gail, 2000; Singer, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both sufficient drive and spatial predictability are the necessary ingredients for the generation of V1 gamma.
source: Overall, our data suggests that both sufficient drive and spatial predictability are the necessary ingredients for the generation of V1 gamma.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Gamma-band oscillations have not been detected in the LGN of awake primates.
source: Furthermore, they have not been detected in the LGN of awake primates (Bastos et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The emergence of gamma oscillations in superficial layers depends on the integration of bottom-up inputs from the LGN and layer four with contextual information mediated through lateral and top-down feedback.
source: Together with the results presented in this paper, this indicates that the emergence of gamma oscillations in superficial layers depends on the integration of bottom-up inputs from the LGN and layer four with contextual information mediated through lateral and top-down feedback.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings combined with previous research.

claim: Superficial layers exhibit strong lateral connectivity and are densely innervated by top-down feedback.
source: Notably, superficial layers exhibit strong lateral connectivity and are densely innervated by top-down feedback (Lund et al., 1993; Barone et al., 2000; Markov et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Within the cortex, the interaction between inhibitory and excitatory neurons likely plays a critical role in gamma rhythmogenesis.
source: Within the cortex, the interaction between inhibitory and excitatory neurons likely plays a critical role (Jadi and Sejnowski, 2014; Veit et al., 2017; Hasenstaub et al., 2005; Buzsáki et al., 2012; Kopell et al., 2000; Whittington et al., 1995; Tiesinga and Sejnowski, 2009; Perrenoud et al., 2016; Cardin et al., 2009; Bartos et al., 2007; Sohal et al., 2009; Womelsdorf et al., 2014; Vinck et al., 2013b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Specialized electrophysiological sub-classes of pyramidal neurons like chattering (fast-rhythmic bursting) cells could be a critical component of gamma rhythmogenesis.
source: Specialized electrophysiological sub-classes of pyramidal neurons like chattering (fast-rhythmic bursting) cells, which have resonant properties in the gamma-frequency band, could also be a critical component of gamma rhythmogenesis (Gray and McCormick, 1996; Cardin et al., 2005; Nowak et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tangential, excitatory connections linking preferentially columns with similar feature preferences may play a crucial role in synchronizing neuronal assemblies coding for related features.
source: Tangential, excitatory connections linking preferentially columns with similar feature preferences (e.g. color or orientation) may play a crucial role in synchronizing neuronal assemblies coding for related features (Vinck and Bosman, 2016; Gray et al., 1989; Korndörfer et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A stimulus with high spatial predictability is likely to simultaneously activate a large number of preferentially coupled columns, which could give rise to enhanced cooperativity among these columns and boost gamma synchronization.
source: A stimulus with high spatial predictability is likely to simultaneously activatea large number of preferentially coupled columns. This could then give rise to enhanced cooperativity among these columns and boost gamma synchronization by the recruitment of local excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the findings.

claim: Feedback from higher visual areas could be critical for gamma synchronization, considering that the spatial spread of tangential connections is somewhat limited.
source: In addition, feedback from higher visual areas could be critical, considering that the spatial spread of tangential connections is somewhat limited and covers a smaller surround region than cortical feedback (Angelucci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Early theories of gamma synchronization proposed that it may contribute to solving the 'binding problem'.
source: Early theories of gamma synchronization proposed that it may contribute to solving the 'binding problem' (Singer and Gray, 1995; Singer, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The activity of distributed neurons can be dynamically grouped together through synchrony according to perceptual Gestalt principles.
source: It was proposed that the activity of distributed neurons can be dynamically grouped together through synchrony according to perceptual Gestalt principles (Milner, 1974; Engel et al., 1992; Singer and Gray, 1995; Singer, 1999; Von Der Malsburg, 1994; Singer, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gamma synchronization can flexibly regulate communication between neuronal populations.
source: Later work emphasized that gamma synchronization can flexibly regulate communication between neuronal populations (Fries, 2005; Salinas and Sejnowski, 2001; Palmigiano et al., 2017; Akam and Kullmann, 2010; Knoblich et al., 2010; Colgin et al., 2009; Jia et al., 2013a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The communication-through-coherence hypothesis states that communication between neuronal populations can be flexibly modulated by selective coherence according to cognitive demands.
source: For example, the communication-through-coherence hypothesis states that communication between neuronal populations can be flexibly modulated by selective coherence according to cognitive demands (Friston, 2005; Fries, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neuronal groups in distant visual areas show gamma-band coherence primarily when they processes an attended stimulus and the level of coherence predicts behavioral benefits of attention.
source: Recent studies have shown that neuronal groups in distant visual areas show gamma-band coherence primarily when they processes an attended stimulus and that the level of coherence predicts behavioral benefits of attention (Gregoriou et al., 2009; Bosman et al., 2012; Grothe et al., 2012; Rohenkohl et al., 2018; Buschman and Miller, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visual cortex shows sparse and gamma-synchronized responses when surround stimulation predicts RF center stimulation.
source: In sum, the present work provides evidence that visual cortex shows sparse and gamma-synchronized responses when surround stimulation predicts RF center stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Firing rates are high when the surround does not predict the center.
source: In contrast, firing rates are high when the surround does not predict the center.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The FSB on which surfaces are displayed strongly modulates gamma synchronization, in a way that suggests that uniform surfaces lead to stronger adaptation of the M-cone compared to L-cone pathways.
source: A second key insight is that the FSB on which surfaces are displayed strongly modulates gamma synchronization, in a way that suggests that uniform surfaces lead to stronger adaptation of the M-cone compared to L-cone pathways.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.
